title: Picard-Lindelof and First-Order Ordinary Differential Equations

items.title: First-order systems, initial value problems, and solutions on intervals
Local Lipschitz continuity in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters
A first-order initial value problem is equivalent to its Volterra integral equation
items.strategy: On an order-convex interval with at least two elements, apply the vector-valued fundamental theorem componentwise to pass from the ODE to the oriented Volterra equation. Conversely, the primitive theorem for a continuous integrand differentiates the integral equation, including the domain-relative endpoints.

items.title: The Picard operator and Picard iterates on a closed ball of continuous curves
Continuous $\mathbb{R}^n$-valued curves on a nonempty compact interval form a complete supremum-metric space
items.strategy: A supremum-metric Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in every coordinate. Completeness of the scalar $C(K,\mathbb R)$ spaces supplies coordinate limits; the finite coordinate list reassembles to a continuous $\mathbb R^n$-valued curve, and equivalence of the Euclidean and maximum norms turns coordinatewise uniform convergence into convergence in the stated supremum metric. Check $n\ge1$ and the one-point interval separately.

items.title: A bounded vector field makes the Picard operator preserve a sufficiently short closed curve ball
items.strategy: A continuous curve gives a continuous composite integrand, so its componentwise integral is again a continuous curve. On a compact time-state cylinder with field bound $M$, the vector integral inequality gives $\|\mathcal T x(t)-x_0\|\le M|t-t_0|\le r$ whenever $hM\le r$. The case $M=0$ is handled without division.

items.title: A state-Lipschitz vector field makes the Picard operator a contraction when $Lh<1$
items.strategy: For two curves in the invariant ball, apply the vector integral inequality and the state-variable Lipschitz bound pointwise. Taking the supremum over $|t-t_0|\le h$ gives $d_\infty(\mathcal T x,\mathcal T y)\le Lh\,d_\infty(x,y)$. The constant-field case $L=0$ and the strict short-time condition are stated explicitly.

items.title: Picard-Lindelöf local existence and uniqueness for first-order systems
items.strategy: Choose a nondegenerate compact cylinder inside the open ODE domain and then choose $h>0$ so that both $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$. The closed curve ball is nonempty and complete, the Picard operator maps it into itself and is a contraction, so Banach gives a unique fixed point. The integral-equation equivalence identifies that fixed point with the unique local solution; interval connectedness propagates local agreement across every common interval.

items.title: Nearby initial values share one Picard–Lindelöf time interval and one state cylinder
items.strategy: Choose nested compact cylinders around the base data. Compactness gives common field and state-Lipschitz bounds, while positive spatial and temporal margins allow one radius and one half-length satisfying the quantitative Picard-Lindelöf hypotheses for every nearby initial point.

items.title: Weissinger's fixed-point criterion for summably contracting iterates
items.strategy: If $\|T^m x-T^m y\|\le a_m\|x-y\|$ and $\sum_{m\ge1}a_m$ converges, telescope the successive iterates to prove they are Cauchy. Completeness gives a limit, continuity follows from the $m=1$ estimate, and the limit is a fixed point. Apply an iterate with $a_m<1$ to prove uniqueness and retain the tail sum as the error bound.

items.title: Picard iteration converges with geometric short-time and factorial cylinder error bounds
items.strategy: On a short interval with $q=Lh<1$, use the short-time contraction lemma before applying the published Banach a priori and a posteriori estimates. On the full invariant cylinder, repeated integration gives $\|\mathcal T^m x-\mathcal T^m y\|_\infty\le (Lh)^m\|x-y\|_\infty/m!$ by induction; Weissinger then yields convergence and the tail bound without requiring $Lh<1$. State the starting iterate at index zero and handle $L=0$ and $h=0$ before division.

items.title: Gronwall's integral inequality with variable and constant coefficients
items.strategy: For forward time, introduce the accumulated integral and multiply it by the integrating factor $exp(-int b)$. Differentiate, integrate the resulting inequality, and divide by the positive factor. State the reflected hypothesis with $int_t^{t_0}$ explicitly and derive the constant-coefficient estimate in both orientations.

items.title: The Grönwall estimate for two solutions of a Lipschitz ODE
items.strategy: Subtract the two Volterra equations, apply the vector integral inequality and the state-Lipschitz estimate, then apply Grönwall to obtain $\|x(t)-y(t)\|\le e^{L|t-t_0|}\|x(t_0)-y(t_0)\|$. Coincident initial values give uniqueness. Check the estimate at $t=t_0$, for $L=0$, and in both time directions.

items.title: Continuous dependence of ODE solutions on initial data and parameters
items.strategy: Choose one compact time-state-parameter cylinder and common field and state-Lipschitz bounds. Apply the quantitative Picard–Lindelöf theorem to each parameter slice with the same radius and time length, then subtract the resulting Volterra equations. Split the integrand into state and parameter discrepancies; compact uniform continuity and Grönwall give the quantitative joint-dependence estimate.

items.title: Extensions, maximal solutions, maximal intervals, and global solutions
Locally unique ODE solutions agree on overlaps and glue across a common endpoint
items.strategy: The set of overlap times on which the two solutions agree is nonempty, closed by continuity, and open by local uniqueness at each agreement point. Since the overlap is an interval it is connected, so the agreement set is the whole overlap. The piecewise union is then well defined; at a common endpoint both derivatives equal the same value of the continuous vector field, so the union is again a solution.

items.title: Every Picard–Lindelöf initial value problem has one maximal solution on an open interval
items.strategy: Take the union of the domains of all local solutions through the initial point. Each domain is an interval containing that point, so their union is an interval; the overlap lemma makes the pointwise union well defined and locally a solution. Its domain is open because local existence extends it around every point, and every other solution is its restriction. No representative is selected from the family.

items.title: A solution whose graph approaches a compact interior region at a finite endpoint extends past that endpoint
items.strategy: A compact subset of the open ODE domain has positive distance from the complement and gives uniform local existence data. If graph points approach a finite endpoint while their states remain in that compact set, extract a convergent state subsequence, use boundedness of the vector field to prove the entire curve has the same endpoint limit, and start a local solution there. The overlap lemma glues it to the old solution.

items.title: At a finite maximal time an ODE solution leaves every compact subset of the domain
items.strategy: If the graph did not eventually leave some compact interior subset, countable choice selects times tending to the finite endpoint with graph points in that compact set, and least later indices give an increasing subsequence. The extension lemma would continue the solution beyond the endpoint, contradicting maximality. State the backward-time version separately and distinguish compact escape from convergence to infinity.

items.title: A globally state-Lipschitz vector field on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ has global solutions
items.strategy: On each finite time slab, continuity bounds $\|F(t,0)\|$ and global state-Lipschitz continuity gives linear growth $\|F(t,x)\|\le M+L\|x\|$. Apply Grönwall to the integral equation to bound the solution on that slab. A finite maximal endpoint would therefore fail the compact-escape criterion, so both maximal endpoints are infinite.

items.title: A scalar first-order linear ODE has a unique solution given by the integrating-factor formula
items.strategy: For continuous $p,q$ on an interval, define $P(x)=\int_{x_0}^x p$ and multiply $y'+py=q$ by $e^P$. The product and chain rules give $(e^P y)'=e^Pq$; integrate and divide by the positive exponential to obtain the formula. Direct differentiation proves existence, while applying the same identity to the difference of two solutions proves uniqueness on the whole interval, including endpoints on either side of $x_0$.

items.title: Euler polygonal approximations for a continuous ODE are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous
items.strategy: For $h>0$ on a cylinder with the given finite field bound $M$, define the Euler polygon recursively at positive-mesh vertices and interpolate linearly. Induction keeps every vertex and segment inside the spatial ball, and every polygon is $M$-Lipschitz, including a shortened final cell.

items.title: A uniformly bounded equicontinuous sequence of $\mathbb R^n$-valued curves on a nonempty compact interval has a uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Fix an enumeration of the rational points of the compact time interval. At each rational time use deterministic nested-box bisection and least admissible indices to extract a convergent subsequence in $\mathbb R^n$; diagonalize over the fixed enumeration. Equicontinuity and a finite rational net make the diagonal subsequence uniformly Cauchy, and completeness of the vector-valued curve space gives a continuous uniform limit. The construction uses no choice principle.

items.title: Peano local existence for a continuous first-order system
items.strategy: Build forward Euler polygons and repeat the construction after reflecting time. Uniform boundedness and equicontinuity yield a uniformly convergent subsequence on each side; uniform continuity controls the Volterra defects and permits passage under the componentwise integral. Glue the two limiting half-solutions at the initial point to obtain the required two-sided local solution.

items.title: Moduli of continuity and the Osgood divergence condition
Osgood's criterion gives uniqueness without a Lipschitz bound
items.strategy: For two solutions with the same initial value, set $R=|x-y|^2$ and bound $|R'|$ by $2sqrt R,ho(sqrt R)$. Put $q_arepsilon=sqrt{R+arepsilon}$, integrate $q_arepsilon'/ho(q_arepsilon)le1$, and let $arepsilon$ tend to zero. Osgood divergence contradicts any positive separation; reflect time and continue through the agreement set.

title: Picard-Lindelof and First-Order Ordinary Differential Equations: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Picard iteration for $y'=y$, $y(0)=1$, recovers the exponential series
items.strategy: Start from the constant curve one and show inductively that the $m$th iterate is $\sum_{k=0}^m t^k/k!$. Cite the published compact-uniform convergence of these iterates to the exponential, and identify the limit as the unique Picard–Lindelöf solution.

items.title: $y'=y^2$, $y(0)=1$, has maximal solution $y(t)=(1-t)^{-1}$ on $(-\infty,1)$
items.strategy: Differentiate the displayed function and check the initial value. Separation or the reciprocal derivative shows that any solution agreeing at zero equals it wherever defined. Its norm tends to infinity as $t\uparrow1$, so the compact-escape criterion makes $(-\infty,1)$ maximal even though the vector field is defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$.

items.title: $y'=2\sqrt{|y|}$ has a continuum of delayed-start solutions through the origin
items.strategy: For every delay $c\ge0$, put $y_c(t)=0$ on $0\le t\le c$ and $y_c(t)=(t-c)^2$ for $t\ge c$. Verify differentiability at the join and the differential equation on both pieces. Distinct delays give distinct solutions with the same initial value; the right-hand side is continuous but fails every local Lipschitz bound at zero.

items.title: The Dirichlet right-hand side gives a first-order equation with no solution
items.strategy: Let $F(t,y)$ be zero for rational $t$ and one for irrational $t$. Any differentiable solution of $y'=F(t,y)$ would have a derivative lacking the intermediate-value property on every interval, contradicting Darboux's theorem for derivatives. The obstruction is independent of the initial value.

items.title: An almost-Lipschitz vector field has a unique solution through zero but is not locally Lipschitz there
items.strategy: Near zero take $f(x)=x(1+|\log|x||)$ with $f(0)=0$ and extend it continuously outside a small interval. Its quotient $|f(x)-f(0)|/|x|$ is unbounded, so it is not locally Lipschitz. It has the Osgood modulus $\rho(r)=r(1+|\log r|)$ and $\int_{0^+}dr/\rho(r)=\infty$, so Osgood's theorem makes the zero solution unique through the origin.

items.title: False: continuity of the right-hand side guarantees unique ODE solutions
items.strategy: Refute the claim with the earlier delayed-start family for $y'=2\sqrt{|y|}$: the right-hand side is continuous, but every delay gives a distinct solution through zero.

items.title: False: a local ODE solution extends across the whole time-domain of its vector field
items.strategy: The polynomial field $F(t,y)=y^2$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$, while the solution through $(0,1)$ is $(1-t)^{-1}$ and has finite maximal endpoint one. The blowup example and compact-escape criterion refute the asserted extension.

items.title: False: local Lipschitz continuity is necessary for uniqueness of an ODE solution
items.strategy: Use the almost-Lipschitz Osgood example: its vector field admits no finite local Lipschitz constant at zero, yet the Osgood divergence condition proves that the zero solution is the unique solution through zero.

title: The Gauge Integral and Cousin's Lemma

items.title: Gauges and gauge-fine tagged partitions of a compact interval
Cousin's lemma: every gauge on a compact interval admits a fine tagged partition
items.strategy: Assume no fine partition exists and bisect the interval, retaining the left half if it still has no fine partition and the right half otherwise. The nested intervals shrink to one point. Eventually a retained interval lies inside the gauge neighborhood of that point and is itself a one-piece fine partition, a contradiction. Treat the degenerate interval separately and choose the tag at the limiting point.

items.title: The Henstock–Kurzweil integral on a compact interval
The Henstock–Kurzweil integral has at most one value
items.strategy: Given two alleged integral values, choose gauges giving error below one third of their distance and take their pointwise minimum. Cousin's lemma supplies a partition fine for both gauges; the triangle inequality puts the two values closer than their distance. Avoid the circular division when the values are already equal.

items.title: Linearity of the Henstock–Kurzweil integral
items.strategy: For a sum, take the pointwise minimum of gauges for the two integrands and split the Riemann-sum error by the triangle inequality. For scalar multiples, separate the zero scalar and otherwise request error $\varepsilon/|c|$. Cousin's lemma prevents either quantified family of fine partitions from being empty.

items.title: Monotonicity of the Henstock–Kurzweil integral
items.strategy: First prove that a nonnegative integrable function has nonnegative integral: every fine Riemann sum is nonnegative, and an assumed negative integral is contradicted by an error smaller than its absolute value. Apply this to $g-f$ and use linearity. Include equality and the degenerate interval convention.

items.title: The Cauchy criterion for Henstock–Kurzweil integrability
items.strategy: Necessity follows by comparing two fine sums with the same integral. For sufficiency, use countable choice to select, for each $n\in\mathbb N$, a gauge $\gamma_n$ for which all fine sums differ by less than $2^{-n}$. Put $\delta_n=\min_{k\le n}\gamma_k$. The nonempty sets of $\delta_n$-fine sums are nested and have diameter below $2^{-n}$; their closed interval hulls are therefore nested with lengths tending to zero, so the nested interval property gives one common value. Every sufficiently fine sum lies near that value. Cousin's lemma supplies nonemptiness, while no sequence of fine partitions is selected.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil integrability on subintervals and additivity over adjacent intervals
items.strategy: For restriction, complete two fine subinterval partitions by one common complementary partition; the whole-interval estimates give the HK Cauchy criterion on each side. Conversely, combine side gauges and shrink them by distance to the cut, so only a cut-tagged cell can cross and it splits validly. Add the side estimates and then orient arbitrary endpoints.

items.title: The Saks–Henstock lemma for fine partial tagged partitions
items.strategy: Fix one whole-interval gauge controlling complete-partition errors before the partial partition is quantified. For a fine partial partition, classify local errors by sign and, on each complementary interval, use a partition fine for the minimum of the fixed gauge and a complement-specific accuracy gauge. Comparing the completed sums with the integral bounds the positive and negative totals separately; combine them to bound the sum of absolute local errors.

items.title: Every Riemann integrable function is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable with the same integral
items.strategy: Use the tagged-partition characterization of the Riemann integral to choose a constant mesh bound. The constant gauge equal to half that bound makes every gauge-fine tagged partition have mesh below the Riemann threshold, so the same Riemann sums converge to the same value. Preserve the universal quantifier over tags and handle the degenerate interval separately.

items.title: Every derivative is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable and satisfies Newton–Leibniz
items.strategy: For each tag, use the least natural reciprocal radius satisfying the derivative estimate, making the gauge canonical without uncountable choice. Split each primitive increment at its tag, sum the two linearization errors, and telescope. This proves the endpoint formula on every nondegenerate compact interval without boundedness of the derivative.

items.title: The indefinite Henstock–Kurzweil integral of a derivative is a primitive
items.strategy: Let $F$ be differentiable on $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, put $f=F'$, and define $G(x)=\int_a^x f$. Apply the derivative form of Newton–Leibniz on each $[a,x]$ to obtain $G(x)=F(x)-F(a)$, with $G(a)=0$ from the degenerate-interval convention. The difference quotient of $G$ at any point of $[a,b]$ is therefore the difference quotient of $F$ there, so $G'=F'=f$, including the one-sided endpoint derivatives used by the library's domain-relative definition.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil integration by parts for differentiable factors
items.strategy: For differentiable $F,G$, the product rule makes $(FG)'=F'G+FG'$, and the derivative theorem makes this sum Henstock–Kurzweil integrable with endpoint integral. If either summand is integrable, linearity makes the other integrable and rearrangement gives the integration-by-parts formula. State the symmetric iff and avoid assuming both products integrable at the outset.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil substitution for a derivative composed with a differentiable map
items.strategy: If $F'=f$ on an interval containing $\phi([a,b])$, the chain rule gives $(F\circ\phi)'=(f\circ\phi)\phi'$. Apply the derivative theorem to the composite to obtain integrability and the endpoint formula. No monotonicity of $\phi$ and no separate integrability hypothesis on $f$ are needed; check constant $\phi$ and reversed endpoint values.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil integrals on half-open and unbounded intervals by compact truncation limits
The Cauchy criterion for a Henstock–Kurzweil integral at a missing endpoint
items.strategy: Apply the ordinary Cauchy criterion for real limits to the truncation primitive $A(c)=\int_a^c f$. Additivity rewrites $A(c'')-A(c')$ as the tail integral. This yields the two-truncation criterion in both finite and infinite endpoint cases; reflect it for a missing left endpoint and treat a finite endpoint already included in the compact domain separately.

items.title: Comparison, absolute-convergence, and limit-comparison tests for noncompact Henstock–Kurzweil integrals
items.strategy: If $|f|\le g$ and $g$ has a convergent noncompact integral, monotonicity bounds every tail integral of $f$ by the corresponding tail integral of $g$; the noncompact Cauchy criterion gives convergence. Taking $g=|f|$ yields absolute convergence. For positive $f,g$ with a finite positive limit of $f/g$, trap the ratio between two positive constants near the missing endpoint and apply comparison in both directions; treat limit zero and infinity as the appropriate one-sided implications.

items.title: Hake's theorem: a finite-endpoint generalized integral is a proper Henstock–Kurzweil integral after assigning the endpoint value
items.strategy: The proper-to-noncompact direction uses Saks-Henstock on an endpoint-tagged tail cell. Conversely, decompose the interval into countably many bands approaching the missing endpoint, choose compatible local gauges with a summable error budget, and shrink them by distances to band boundaries. Every global fine partition then splits into complete bands, one final partial band, and an endpoint-tagged tail cell, whose errors are controlled separately.

title: The Gauge Integral and Cousin's Lemma: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The indicator of the irrationals is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable with integral $1$
items.strategy: Enumerate the rationals in $[0,1]$ and choose the gauge at the $k$th rational so its interval length contributes less than $\varepsilon 2^{-k}$. Give irrational tags an unrestricted small positive radius. In any fine partition the total length of intervals with rational tags is below $\varepsilon$; the Riemann sum of the irrational indicator therefore differs from one by less than $\varepsilon$. Then prove non-Riemann-integrability locally: density of the rationals and irrationals makes every lower Darboux sum zero and every upper Darboux sum one.

items.title: $F(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)$ has an unbounded derivative whose Henstock–Kurzweil integral is $\sin 1$
items.strategy: Set $F(0)=0$ and differentiate for $x>0$ to obtain $F'(x)=2x\sin(1/x^2)-2x^{-1}\cos(1/x^2)$, with $F'(0)=0$. Exhibit sequences on which the second term is unbounded. The derivative theorem gives Henstock–Kurzweil integrability on $[0,1]$ and evaluates the integral as $F(1)-F(0)=\sin1$.

items.title: $\sin x/x$ has a Henstock–Kurzweil integral on $[0,\infty)$
items.strategy: Assign the removable value one at zero. Every compact restriction is continuous, hence Riemann and Henstock–Kurzweil integrable. The primitive of $\sin x$ is bounded and $1/x$ is nonnegative, decreasing, and tends to zero, so the published Dirichlet test gives convergence of the compact truncation integrals. The noncompact definition therefore yields an HK integral; do not claim the unproved value $\pi/2$.

items.title: Cousin's lemma yields the Heine–Borel theorem on a compact interval
items.strategy: Given an open cover of $[a,b]$, choose for each point a gauge radius whose centered interval lies in one covering set. A fine tagged partition exists by Cousin's lemma, and the finitely many covering sets selected at its tags cover every partition subinterval and hence all of $[a,b]$. The empty and one-point intervals are handled before choosing tags.

items.title: False: every derivative is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: Use the earlier example $F(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)$: its derivative is unbounded near zero, while the definition of the Riemann integral requires boundedness. This directly refutes the universal claim. The Henstock–Kurzweil derivative theorem supplies the correct replacement and evaluates the same derivative by endpoint difference. Mention the stronger published bounded Volterra witness only in a non-load-bearing Remark.

items.title: False: every Henstock–Kurzweil integrable function is bounded
items.strategy: The derivative of $x^2\sin(1/x^2)$ is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable on $[0,1]$ but unbounded near zero, as established in the earlier example.

items.title: Henstock–Kurzweil integrability does not imply integrability of the absolute value
items.strategy: Use the derivative of $x^2sin(1/x^2)$. On compact intervals away from zero, $|f|$ is continuous and hence locally HK integrable. Endpoint increments on alternating sine extrema give a harmonic lower bound for the truncation integrals of $|f|$; Hake then rules out proper HK integrability on $[0,1]$.

items.title: False: Henstock–Kurzweil integrability implies Riemann integrability
items.strategy: Use the preceding example, which establishes both that the irrational indicator has Henstock–Kurzweil integral one and that its lower and upper Darboux integrals are zero and one. The same function is therefore Henstock–Kurzweil integrable but not Riemann integrable, directly refuting the converse of the Riemann-to-HK theorem.

items.title: False: every Henstock–Kurzweil integrable function is a derivative
items.strategy: The indicator of the irrationals is Henstock–Kurzweil integrable but has only the values zero and one on every interval. It therefore fails the intermediate-value property, whereas Darboux's theorem says every derivative has that property.
